metaTitle: Ticks in Wisconsin: Types, Lyme Map, Season
metaDescription: Deer ticks are established in 61 of 72 Wisconsin counties, and the state had 6,283 Lyme cases in 2023. Tick photos, a county Lyme map, season and ID help.
h1: Ticks in Wisconsin: Species, County Maps, Lyme Data and Tick Season
dek: Which ticks live in Wisconsin, where Lyme disease is most common county by county, when each tick is active, and what the state offers if you find one.
excerpt: Blacklegged ticks are established in 61 of Wisconsin's 72 counties. Species photos, Lyme rates by county, tick season by month and where to get a tick identified.

quickAnswer.lead: **The blacklegged (deer) tick, which spreads Lyme disease, is established in 61 of Wisconsin's 72 counties, and the state reported 6,283 Lyme cases in 2023, the fifth most of any state**, according to [CDC surveillance data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/surveillance-data-1.html). The American dog tick, or wood tick, is the one residents find most often, but UW–Madison says it has not been linked to disease transmission in Wisconsin.
bullets: CDC's county table, which runs through December 2025, lists blacklegged ticks as established in 61 counties and reported in 7 more, and the state health department says deer ticks are present in all 72.

Relative to population, 2023 Lyme rates were highest in northern, central and western counties such as Florence, Jackson and Pepin, and lowest in the south and east, including Milwaukee, Kenosha and Racine.
The state counted 8,930 Lyme cases in 2025, its most on record, but says a new electronic route for reporting rashes diagnosed by health care providers largely explains the jump from 2024.
Wisconsin reported 18 Powassan virus disease cases in 2025, more than any other state, and a record 1,076 anaplasmosis cases.
Ticks are most active from April through September; deer tick nymphs peak from late May into July, and adults are active in spring and again in fall.
As of October 2026, the state identifies ticks from residents' photos but cannot say whether a tick carried germs, and the Asian longhorned tick had not been found in Wisconsin as of April 2026.

body.text: Which ticks live in Wisconsin?

Sixteen hard tick species have been reported in Wisconsin, according to [UW–Madison's page on other tick species found in the state](https://wisconsin-ticks.russell.wisc.edu/other-ticks/), but many of them feed mainly on wildlife and rarely bite people. Three account for nearly all the ticks residents find: the American dog tick (also called the wood tick), the blacklegged tick (also called the deer tick) and, far behind, the lone star tick.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) sees that balance in its Tick Identification Service. In 2026, through the week of September 28, the service had received 525 submissions of American dog ticks, 266 of blacklegged ticks and 41 of lone star ticks from Wisconsin residents, plus 26 of insects or spiders and 37 listed as not identified, according to the department's [tick surveillance report for that week](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/publications/p03757-2026-39.pdf). Its own field surveillance concentrates on the blacklegged tick, which it calls the most important carrier of human tick-borne infections in Wisconsin.

body.alt: Three blacklegged ticks on a blue-green surface: a large adult female with a reddish-orange body and dark shield, and two much smaller immature ticks
body.caption: Blacklegged tick adult female (top) and two immature ticks, a nymph and a larva. DHS says that usually only nymphs and adult females spread illness.
body.credit: CDC/ Michael L. Levin, Ph. D. (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: The blacklegged tick is the one that matters most for health. The [DHS page about Lyme disease](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/tick/lyme-about.htm) says it spreads the disease, that deer ticks are present in all counties in Wisconsin, and that most people are infected by nymphs, the immature stage, which are about the size of a poppy seed. Lyme disease is caused by the bacterium *Borrelia burgdorferi* and, rarely, *Borrelia mayonii*. To compare sizes and markings across species, see [how to tell the common US ticks apart](/blog/what-do-ticks-look-like).

The American dog tick is the one most people meet. [UW–Madison's wood tick page](https://wisconsin-ticks.russell.wisc.edu/wisconsin-ticks/dermacentor-variabilis/) says the adults are very common on people, dogs and cats, while the larvae and nymphs almost never bite people. It adds that diseases from wood tick bites are rare in Wisconsin and that this tick has not been associated with disease transmission in the state, although it can transmit the bacteria behind Rocky Mountain spotted fever and tularemia in other parts of the US. The Lyme bacterium has been found in wood ticks, but there is no scientific evidence that they can pass it on.

body.alt: Adult female American dog tick on a blade of grass, reddish-brown with a cream-and-brown mottled shield behind the head and pale-banded legs
body.caption: Adult female American dog tick, or wood tick: the tick Wisconsin residents send to the state most often.
body.credit: CDC/DVBID/ Gary O. Maupin; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: The rest matter less for people. *Ixodes cookei*, which feeds mostly on small and medium-sized mammals, is not very common in Wisconsin but occasionally bites people, and UW–Madison says it may transmit the germs behind Powassan virus disease and Lyme disease. The brown dog tick, which can complete its life cycle indoors, is extremely rare in the state. The rabbit tick typically does not feed on people, and *Ixodes texanus*, found mostly on raccoons, only very occasionally bites people or pets.

body.alt: Engorged female Ixodes cookei tick on a wooden surface, its swollen body pale blue-gray behind a small reddish-brown shield and reddish-brown legs
body.caption: An engorged female *Ixodes cookei*, often called the groundhog or woodchuck tick. UW–Madison says it is not very common in Wisconsin but occasionally bites people.
body.credit: (c) adamfritz, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Where are blacklegged ticks found in Wisconsin?

Nearly everywhere. [CDC's county surveillance table](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/tick-surveillance-data-sets.html), which runs through December 31, 2025, lists blacklegged ticks as established in 61 of Wisconsin's 72 counties and reported in 7 more: Dodge, Florence, Outagamie, Ozaukee, Polk, Shawano and Winnebago. Calumet, Iron, Kewaunee and Washington counties have no record. Established means six or more ticks of one life stage, or more than one life stage, were collected in a county within 12 months; reported means fewer than six of one life stage. To compare other states, see [tick maps and Lyme data for every state](/learn/ticks-by-state).

body.title: Blacklegged (deer) tick status by county, Wisconsin, through 2025
body.caption: Established means six or more blacklegged ticks of one life stage, or more than one life stage, were collected in the county within 12 months; reported means fewer. No record does not mean no ticks: it can mean no one has sampled there, and DHS says deer ticks are present in every county. Status is cumulative.
body.source: [CDC ArboNET Tick Module (county status through Dec 31, 2025)](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/tick-surveillance-data-sets.html)

body.text: Read the map as a record of collecting, not of risk. CDC says a county with no records should not be taken as free of the tick, because the gap can reflect a lack of sampling, and DHS says deer ticks are present in every Wisconsin county. Florence County, listed only as reported, had the state's highest Lyme disease rate in 2023 (see the county map below). Status is also cumulative: once a county is established, it stays that way.

body.alt: Adult female blacklegged tick with a reddish-brown body beside a much smaller nymph on a person's fingertip, showing how small the nymph is
body.caption: An adult female blacklegged tick (left) and a nymph (right) on a fingertip, for scale. At the state's sampling sites, nymphs are most numerous from late May into July.
body.credit: CDC/ Division of Vector-Borne Diseases Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch; photo: Lauren Bishop (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Which germs have been found in Wisconsin ticks?

CDC's companion table records where each germ has been found in host-seeking blacklegged ticks, meaning ticks hunting for a host rather than feeding on one. It is cumulative, and a county without a record is not proof the germ is absent.

body.text: The Lyme bacterium's 41 counties stretch from Bayfield and Ashland on Lake Superior to Walworth on the Illinois line, and the anaplasmosis and babesiosis germs have each been recorded in more than 20 counties.
Is the lone star tick in Wisconsin?

It turns up, but whether it has settled in depends on whom you ask. [UW–Madison's lone star tick page](https://wisconsin-ticks.russell.wisc.edu/wisconsin-ticks/amblyomma-americanum-lone-star-tick/) says the species does not yet have an established population in Wisconsin. It is rarely found, though there are submissions every year, especially from the southern half of the state but as far north as Douglas County. The researchers think a few ticks most likely arrive on migrating birds each year and survive the summer, but not a Wisconsin winter.

CDC's tick surveillance data (ArboNET Tick Module) read differently: through 2025, they list the lone star tick as established in one Wisconsin county, Dane, and reported in 26 others. The two are not measuring the same thing. CDC calls a county established once six or more ticks of one life stage, or more than one life stage, have been collected there within 12 months, and the label stays in later years. UW–Madison is judging whether the tick breeds here and survives the winter, and it says its own map of counties with a lone star record does not mean the tick is established and breeding there.

Residents do find them. The DHS identification service received 41 lone star tick submissions from Wisconsin residents in 2026 through the week of September 28, about 1 in 20 of the ticks it identified, according to the [department's late-September surveillance report](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/publications/p03757-2026-39.pdf).

body.alt: Adult female lone star tick on a green leaf, reddish-brown with long mouthparts and a single pale spot in the middle of its back
body.caption: Adult female lone star tick, named for the single pale spot on its back. UW–Madison says it is rarely found in Wisconsin.
body.credit: CDC/ Dr. Amanda Loftis, Dr. William Nicholson, Dr. Will Reeves, Dr. Chris Paddock; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Lyme disease is not the main worry with this tick: UW–Madison says transmission of the Lyme bacterium by lone star ticks has not been confirmed. The species is the main carrier of the bacteria behind two forms of ehrlichiosis, and the same page reports evidence of infection with one of them, *Ehrlichia chaffeensis*, in Wisconsin residents with no travel history, although DHS says most Wisconsin residents infected with it caught it while traveling to other states. Research also suggests its bite can leave some people allergic to red meat, a condition called alpha-gal syndrome, with symptoms UW–Madison says range from hives to severe shock; see [alpha-gal syndrome and the tick bites linked to it](/blog/alpha-gal-syndrome).
Has the Asian longhorned tick reached Wisconsin?

Not as of April 2026. [UW–Madison Extension](https://livestock.extension.wisc.edu/2026/04/14/livestock-producers-encouraged-to-be-on-the-lookout-for-asian-longhorned-ticks/) said then that the tick had not been identified in Wisconsin, although it had been found in neighboring Michigan, Illinois and Iowa within the previous two years and research suggests Wisconsin's climate is suitable for it. First identified in the US in New Jersey in 2017, it has spread mainly as an unnoticed passenger on cattle and other livestock moved around the country, and its females can reproduce without mating.

Extension says ticks found on livestock can be submitted to a veterinarian or to the UW–Madison Department of Entomology for identification. A tick found on a person or a pet can also go to the DHS photo identification service described below.
How much Lyme disease does Wisconsin have?

More than any other Midwestern state. Wisconsin reported 6,283 Lyme disease cases in 2023, a rate of 106.9 per 100,000 residents, according to [CDC's Lyme disease surveillance data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/surveillance-data-1.html). Only New York, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and New Jersey reported more, Wisconsin's cases made up about 7% of the US total, and its rate ranked ninth among the states.

body.title: Reported Lyme disease cases in Wisconsin, 2008 to 2023
body.yLabel: Cases per year, by state of residence
body.caption: A revised case definition took effect in 2022, so 2022 and 2023 are not directly comparable with earlier years. CDC says COVID-19 left 2019 and 2020 data incomplete in some states. The state's own yearly totals for 2012 to 2021 run higher because its [tracking data](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/epht/lyme.htm) add estimated cases. Data through 2023, the latest CDC year as of October 2026.

body.text: Read the jump after 2021 with care. DHS says its current case definition, in effect since January 1, 2022, relies largely on laboratory data alone, where the old one leaned on a combination of laboratory and clinical information. Fewer criteria are now needed for a report to count as a case, which raised counts statewide and in most counties, so figures from 2022 on are not directly comparable with 2021 or earlier, according to the department's [Lyme disease tracking page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/epht/lyme.htm).

The state's newer counts are higher still. The department's downloadable data show 6,469 cases in 2024 and 8,930 in 2025 (its Lyme data page says 8,929), the most in records going back to 1991, a rate of 149.5 per 100,000 residents. DHS says most of the increase from 2024 to 2025 can be explained by a reporting change: in 2025 it began receiving reports of rashes diagnosed by health care providers through electronic case reporting, which was introduced to close gaps in reporting. For 2023 the state's own count is 6,379; this page uses CDC's 6,283 for the years CDC has published.
How does Wisconsin compare with its neighbors?
Wisconsin's 2023 count was more than double Minnesota's and more than five times Michigan's, while Illinois and Iowa reported a few hundred cases each. Minnesota's rate was about half of Wisconsin's.

body.text: Which Wisconsin counties have the most Lyme disease?

Relative to population, counties across the north, the center and the west. In 2023, Florence, Jackson and Pepin counties each recorded more than 500 cases per 100,000 residents, about five times the statewide rate, and 20 more counties were between 250 and 499. The map shows the 2023 rate for every county, calculated by BuzzSkito from [CDC's county-level Lyme data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/lyme-disease-case-map.html) and the [Census Bureau's county population estimates](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-counties-total.html).

body.title: Lyme disease cases per 100,000 residents by county, Wisconsin, 2023
body.caption: Confirmed and probable cases by county of residence. Rates are BuzzSkito's calculation: CDC's 2023 county counts divided by the Census Bureau's July 1, 2023 population estimates (Vintage 2025). CDC's county file places 6,079 of Wisconsin's 6,283 cases in a county, and CDC's statewide rate rests on a smaller population figure, so these rates run slightly below CDC's statewide figure (102.5 against 106.9). Small counties swing sharply: Florence County's 27 cases came from about 4,700 people.
body.source: [CDC county-level Lyme disease data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/lyme-disease-case-map.html), 2023; [U.S. Census Bureau county population estimates](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-counties-total.html)

body.text: Raw counts follow population instead. Dane County, home to Madison, had the most cases in 2023 (295), followed by Waukesha (268), Marathon (245) and Eau Claire (229), yet Dane's rate of 50.9 per 100,000 was less than half the state's. Rates were lowest in the south and east: Lafayette (17.6), Milwaukee (21.6), Kenosha (26.2) and Racine (27.9) counties had the four lowest.

Two cautions apply to any county figure. Cases are counted where the patient lives, which is not necessarily where the bite happened, as [CDC's Lyme case map page](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/lyme-disease-case-map.html) notes, and DHS adds that some infections are picked up while traveling. And small counties swing from year to year: Florence County's rate rests on 27 cases among about 4,700 residents, Lafayette's on 3.
Which other tick-borne diseases occur in Wisconsin?

Anaplasmosis comes next. DHS calls it the second most common illness spread by ticks in Wisconsin, after Lyme disease. The state averaged 617 confirmed and probable cases a year from 2016 through 2025, and 2025 brought 1,076, the most ever documented in Wisconsin, according to the department's [anaplasmosis data page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/tick/anaplasmosis-data.htm). Cases are most common in June and July and are reported most often among people living in the northern, western and northeastern regions. CDC's table records the germ's human-active variant in blacklegged ticks from 24 counties.

Powassan virus disease is rare, but Wisconsin reports more of it than almost any other state. [CDC's Powassan virus data](https://www.cdc.gov/powassan/data-maps/historic-data.html) show 85 Wisconsin cases from 2004 through 2025, second only to Minnesota's 89, including 12 in 2024 and 18 in 2025, the most of any state that year. Of the 85, 76 were neuroinvasive, which CDC describes as the severe form; it notes that milder illness is more likely to go unreported. CDC's tick table records Powassan virus in blacklegged ticks from 7 Wisconsin counties.

body.title: Reported Powassan virus disease cases in Wisconsin, 2004 to 2025
body.caption: Neuroinvasive and non-neuroinvasive cases combined, counted where patients live, not where they were infected; years without a bar had no reported cases. CDC says its data for 2004 to 2025 were finalized on September 16, 2026.

body.text: Other germs travel with Wisconsin's deer ticks too. CDC's table records *Babesia microti*, the cause of babesiosis, in ticks from 22 counties; *Borrelia miyamotoi*, the cause of hard tick relapsing fever, in 28; and *Ehrlichia muris eauclairensis*, a cause of ehrlichiosis, in 6.
When is tick season in Wisconsin?

Mainly April through September, but exposure can happen in any month. The [DHS page on ticks in Wisconsin](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/tick/wisconsin.htm) says ticks are most active during the warmer months, April to September, and that tick exposure can occur year-round. The two stages that usually spread illness, nymphs and adult females, peak at different times: deer tick nymphs from late May into July, and adults in spring and again in fall.

DHS tracks the season in the field. About every other week from March through November, its staff pull a white denim drag cloth along a path about 2,460 feet (750 meters) long at sentinel sites in Iowa, Lincoln and Waupaca counties and collect the ticks that cling to it. In 2026, adult deer ticks peaked in mid-April, nymphs were most numerous from late May through July, and larvae peaked in early August; by the end of September adults were increasing again, the [department's late-September report](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/publications/p03757-2026-39.pdf) shows. Its charts for 2025 show adults collected again from October into November.

body.text: Where can you get a tick identified in Wisconsin?

Through the DHS Tick Identification Service. The [department's tick data page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/tick/wisconsin.htm) says residents of Wisconsin, Illinois, Iowa, Michigan and Minnesota can answer a few questions and submit photographs online to have a tick identified. As of October 2026, the service cannot determine whether the tick was carrying germs or whether it made you sick.

DHS says the only way to know whether a tick made you sick is an evaluation, and sometimes a blood test, by a health care provider. Identification still helps: knowing whether it was a deer tick, the tick that spreads Lyme disease in Wisconsin, gives your provider something concrete, so photograph a tick before you dispose of it.
What should you do after a tick bite in Wisconsin?

Remove the tick right away, consider calling a health care provider promptly about a single preventive antibiotic dose, and watch your health for 30 days. The [DHS tick bite prevention page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/tick/bite-prevention.htm) describes removal this way:

items: Grasp the tick with narrow-bladed tweezers as close to the skin as possible; if you have none, cover your fingers with tissue paper or rubber gloves.
Pull up and out with steady, firm pressure.
Clean the bite with rubbing alcohol, then wash your hands with soap and water.
Do not twist, squeeze, crush or puncture the tick, and do not put petroleum jelly, a hot match or nail polish on it.

body.text: For a fuller walk-through, see [the step-by-step tick removal guide](/blog/how-to-remove-tick-safely).

[DHS's tick data page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/tick/wisconsin.htm) suggests that anyone bitten who lives in Wisconsin, where Lyme disease is common, consider contacting a health care provider right away to see whether a single dose of antibiotics may be appropriate. Its [Lyme disease page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/tick/lyme-about.htm) says preventive treatment must be taken within 72 hours of removing the tick, and [CDC says](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/causes/index.html) a tick usually must be attached for more than 24 hours to spread Lyme disease, so quick removal counts. A provider decides whether the dose fits your case.

Then watch for symptoms. DHS asks people to monitor themselves for a rash, fever, new muscle and joint pain and new fatigue for 30 days after a bite, and to call a provider at once if any appear. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/signs-symptoms/index.html) lists early Lyme symptoms 3 to 30 days after the bite: fever, chills, headache, fatigue, muscle and joint aches and swollen lymph nodes.

The rash appears in about 70% to 80% of cases, expands over days or weeks, and can look reddish, gray or purple depending on skin tone; it may clear in the center as it grows. A small bump or redness at the bite site is common and usually fades in one to two days. [The stages of Lyme disease symptoms](/blog/lyme-disease-symptoms-guide) covers what can follow if it goes untreated.

body.alt: Erythema migrans rash on the back of an upper arm: a dark red center, a paler middle band and a red outer ring, the bull's-eye pattern
body.caption: Erythema migrans, the expanding rash of early Lyme disease, in its bull's-eye form. DHS notes that the rash can look reddish, gray or purple depending on skin tone, and that it may clear in the center as it grows.
body.credit: CDC/ James Gathany; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.title: See a health care provider if you feel ill
body.text: A rash, fever, new muscle or joint pain, or new fatigue in the 30 days after a tick bite is a reason to call a provider and mention the tick. This page summarizes what public health agencies publish and is not a diagnosis.
How do you prevent tick bites in Wisconsin?

Use repellent, treat clothing with permethrin, keep to the middle of trails and check everyone, pets included, after time outdoors. The [DHS tick bite prevention page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/tick/bite-prevention.htm) recommends:

items: **Repellent on skin and clothing.** The department lists products with 20% to 30% DEET, 10% to 20% picaridin, 15% to 20% IR3535 or 30% to 40% oil of lemon eucalyptus. Do not use oil of lemon eucalyptus on children under 3, and apply repellent to children yourself, avoiding their hands, eyes and mouth.
**Permethrin on clothes, not skin.** Treat clothing, shoes and gear; the treatment lasts through several washes.
**Covered, light-colored clothing.** Wear long sleeves, long pants and tall socks, tuck your shirt into your pants and your pants into your socks or shoes, and tape the gap for long days outdoors.
**The middle of the trail.** Walk in the center, avoid brushing against plants at the edge, and stay out of brushy areas with tall grass and leaf litter.

**Checks, a shower and the dryer.** Check your whole body after being outdoors, including in your own yard: armpits, behind the knees, scalp, in and around the ears, inside the belly button and the groin. Shower within two hours of coming inside, and tumble dry clothes on high heat for 10 minutes, or 60 minutes if they are damp.

body.text: Around the house, DHS suggests clearing tall grass, brush and leaf litter, mowing often, putting a barrier of wood chips or gravel between lawn and woods (CDC recommends one 3 feet wide), keeping play equipment in a sunny spot away from the woods, not feeding deer, and stacking firewood neatly in a dry place away from the house. It also mentions a spring application of a tick-killing pesticide, following federal and state pesticide rules.

Pets bring ticks indoors as well. DHS advises checking pets, clothing and gear before going inside and using a tick treatment your veterinarian recommends. Our guide to [ticks on dogs](/blog/ticks-on-dogs) covers checks and removal on pets.

faqs.question: Do wood ticks carry Lyme disease in Wisconsin?
faqs.answer: There is no evidence that they can pass it on. UW–Madison's tick researchers say the Lyme bacterium has been found in wood ticks, also called American dog ticks, but there is no scientific evidence that they can transmit it, and the tick has not been associated with disease transmission in Wisconsin. Elsewhere in the US it can spread Rocky Mountain spotted fever and tularemia. In Wisconsin, Lyme disease is spread by the blacklegged, or deer, tick, so it helps to know which tick bit you.

faqs.question: Are ticks active in Wisconsin in the winter?
faqs.answer: Tick exposure can occur year-round, the state health department says, although ticks are most active from April through September. Adult deer ticks are most active in the cooler months: at the state's sampling sites they peak in spring and return in fall, and in 2025 they were still being collected in November. The department advises caution throughout the year, so check for ticks after time in woods, brush or leaf litter on mild days.

faqs.question: Which Wisconsin county has the most Lyme disease?
faqs.answer: It depends on whether you count cases or rates. Dane County had the most cases in 2023, 295, because so many people live there. Relative to population, Florence County was highest, at about 576 cases per 100,000 residents, followed by Jackson and Pepin counties, based on CDC county counts and Census population estimates. Cases are counted where patients live, not where they were bitten, and small counties can swing sharply from year to year.

faqs.question: Can I get a tick tested for Lyme disease in Wisconsin?
faqs.answer: Not through the state's identification service. As of October 2026, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services identifies ticks from photos submitted online, but the service cannot tell whether a tick carried germs or made you sick. The department says the only way to know whether a tick made you sick is an evaluation, and sometimes a blood test, by a health care provider. After a bite, the department suggests Wisconsin residents consider asking a provider promptly about a single preventive antibiotic dose, which must be taken within 72 hours of removing the tick.

faqs.question: How many Lyme disease cases did Wisconsin have in 2025?
faqs.answer: The state health department counted 8,930 confirmed and probable cases in 2025, the most in its records, which go back to 1991, or about 149.5 per 100,000 residents. It says most of the increase from 2024, when it counted 6,469, came from a reporting change: rashes diagnosed by health care providers began reaching the state through electronic case reporting. As of October 2026, CDC's published state figures ran only through 2023, when Wisconsin reported 6,283 cases.

faqs.question: Is the lone star tick established in Wisconsin?
faqs.answer: It depends on the definition. UW–Madison's tick researchers say the species does not yet have an established population in the state, while CDC's surveillance data, which count a county as established once a collection threshold is met, list one county, Dane, as established through 2025. Lone star ticks are found every year, mostly in the southern half of Wisconsin but as far north as Douglas County, and most likely arrive on migrating birds without surviving the winter. The state's identification service had received 41 from residents in 2026 as of early October. Lyme transmission by this tick has not been confirmed, but research suggests its bite can trigger a red meat allergy, alpha-gal syndrome.
